solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hike — second by rugby forwards

parts.note: to second a motion is to back it
the forwards in a rugby team are called the pack

explanation.surface: A terse note pairing a hike with a moment of support from the rugby forwards.
explanation.walkthrough: "Second" reads as a unit of time or a runner-up, but here it is the verb: to second a proposal is to back it.
explanation.definitionFit: To backpack is to hike with your gear on your back.

clue.text: Drill — dull activity

definitions.meaning: the verb: to make a hole with a turning tool
a noun for something tedious that wears you out

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses share the spelling: to bore a hole is to drill, and a bore is something tedious.
explanation.definitionFit: Bore is both a verb meaning to drill and a noun for a tedious thing.

clue.text: Is able to party, pure at heart? There's frankness

parts.note: one who is able to do something can do it
a do is a party

indicators.note: the heart of 'pure' is its middle, so only its central letters are kept

parts.note: the middle two letters of PURE

explanation.surface: Someone who can throw a party while staying pure of heart is praised for their honesty.
explanation.walkthrough: "Party" is the short slang DO, as in a birthday do.
explanation.definitionFit: Candour is openness and honesty, which is frankness.

clue.text: Uproar in opium den man resolved

indicators.note: to resolve something is to break it down and settle it anew, so the letters are worked out into a new order

parts.note: the letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: A disturbance in an opium den that one man finally settles.
explanation.walkthrough: "Resolved" looks like the man settling the row, but it tells you to rework the eleven letters of OPIUM DEN MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: Milton coined the word for the capital of Hell, and it now means any scene of noisy chaos.

clue.text: My final ice-cream holder?

parts.note: "Cor!" is a British exclamation of surprise, like "My!"
a net figure is the final one after deductions

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether this is their last ice-cream cone.
explanation.walkthrough: "My" reads as a possessive but is the exclamation, and COR is the British slang version. The question mark flags the playful whole.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a cornet is the cone that holds ice cream.

clue.text: Objections over this residual part of ticket

indicators.note: in a down-reading sense 'over' means turned over, so the word is flipped

parts.note: objections are ifs and buts

explanation.surface: People object to the torn-off bit left from a ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: Objections are BUTS, as in 'no ifs or buts'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stub is the part of a ticket you keep after the rest is torn off.

clue.text: Initially tied with ideal new English string

indicators.note: 'initially' asks for the opening letter of each following word

parts.note: first letters of tied, with, ideal, new, English

explanation.surface: A parcel first tied up with the perfect new English string.
explanation.walkthrough: "Initially" looks like it means "at first" in the story, but it applies to every word after it, all five of which supply a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: twine is string made of strands twisted together, the kind used to tie parcels.

clue.text: Short pause about to be welcomed by swimmer

parts.note: someone who bathes in the sea is a bather
re means about, as in a memo

explanation.surface: A swimmer is about to stop for a short rest.
explanation.walkthrough: "About to" reads as one phrase meaning "going to"; split it, because "about" is a piece of wordplay and "to be welcomed by" is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: you take a pause to catch your breath, hence the name.

clue.text: Including name, destroy argument

parts.note: to destroy is to ruin
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Mentioning someone by name wrecks the case you were making.
explanation.walkthrough: The container indicator comes first, so RUIN has to be found before it can include N.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: having a run-in with someone means clashing with them in a row.

clue.text: Salesman with hat one loathed

parts.note: a sales rep
tile is old slang for a hat

explanation.surface: A salesman in a hat is someone everybody detests.
explanation.walkthrough: TILE for a hat is dated British slang, still common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A reptile is a contemptible, loathsome person.

clue.text: Pet Patricia trained to become actively involved

indicators.note: a trained pet has been reshaped, so the letters are reshaped too

parts.note: the letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: Patricia's pet has been trained so it can join in.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pet" looks like an animal or a term of endearment, but it is just three more letters for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To participate is to take an active part.

clue.text: Too serious about sensitivity to music at home

parts.note: over means about, as in arguing over something
an ear for music
a nest is a bird's home

explanation.surface: Someone takes their feel for music far too solemnly while at home.
explanation.walkthrough: "About" is usually RE or C; here it is OVER. "At home" gives NEST, the home itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: earnest is serious, and the over- prefix supplies the "too".

clue.text: Spend about a pound on identity document? Brilliant!

indicators.note: SPEND goes around the pound sign, surrounding it

parts.note: the word as printed
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra
ID is short for an identity document

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted to spend just a pound on an ID card.
explanation.walkthrough: "Spend" is not a definition but the outer letters themselves, and "about" puts L inside them rather than meaning roughly.
explanation.definitionFit: Splendid is an exclamation of delight, like brilliant.

clue.text: Excuse average teacher

parts.note: par is the normal or average level
a don is a university teacher at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.walkthrough: "Excuse" is the verb here, as in excuse a fault.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: both mean to forgive or let off a fault, and "excuse me" and "pardon me" are interchangeable too.

clue.text: Uncomplicated foreign article on PM is backed

indicators.note: the article sits after the rest, placed on it
to back up is to go backwards, so PM IS is written back to front

parts.note: as printed
as printed
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A newspaper line: a foreign piece of writing supports the Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: "Backed" reads as supported, but it reverses PM IS; "article" is the grammatical kind, and foreign makes it French LE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both adjectives describe something easy to understand, with no complex parts.

clue.text: Biro, say? It's not on birth certificate

definitions.meaning: Biro is a brand of ballpoint, so it is the name of a pen
a writer's pseudonym is not their registered name

explanation.walkthrough: Biro is a brand of ballpoint, so it is literally the name of a pen; the question mark admits the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen name is a writer's pseudonym, which never appears on a birth certificate.

clue.text: Playful remarks coming from drab anteroom

indicators.note: the answer comes out of the words that follow, lifted straight from them

parts.note: draB ANTERoom

explanation.surface: Light-hearted chatter drifts out of a dull waiting room.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans the gap between the two words, starting with the last letter of "drab".
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word covers good-humoured teasing exchanged between friends.

clue.text: Pro equality, anti regalia possibly?

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the letters might be arranged some other way

parts.note: the letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: Someone for equality would surely be against royal regalia.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fair description of the answer too: a believer in equality may well object to regalia, the trappings of royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym used as an adjective: the word comes from French égal, equal, and describes a belief that all people deserve equal rights.

clue.text: Fruit, bacon, unlimited by Royal Navy

indicators.note: without limits means without its boundary letters, so only the inside of bacon stays

parts.note: BACON without its first and last letters
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A breakfast list: fruit, plenty of bacon, courtesy of the Navy.
explanation.walkthrough: "Unlimited" suggests endless bacon, but it strips BACON of its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A botanical sense: the oak's nut counts as its fruit, though "fruit" first suggests something sweet.

clue.text: Article new at that time

parts.note: the definite article
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A piece of writing that was fresh at the time.
explanation.walkthrough: "Article" suggests a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical article THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the adverb points back to a moment in the past or future, as in "I lived there then".

clue.text: Motor ad wrong — he won't complain

indicators.note: letters that are wrong are out of their proper order

parts.note: the letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: A car advert has an error, but one viewer will not grumble about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description rather than a synonym: a doormat is walked over without protest.
explanation.definitionFit: A doormat is a person who lets others treat them badly without complaint.

clue.text: Mortify a Bachelor of Arts, quiet

parts.note: as printed
the degree abbreviation
sh is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: A quiet graduate is made to feel embarrassed.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are read in clue order; the only trap is taking "a" as filler when it supplies the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: both mean to make someone feel ashamed; mortify is the stronger word.

clue.text: Eat, recalling Blyton maybe

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Enid Blyton was a British children's author; maybe marks her as one example of an Enid

explanation.surface: Someone eats while remembering the children's books of Enid Blyton.
explanation.walkthrough: "Recalling" reads as remembering, but it sends ENID backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly formal: dining is having a meal, usually the main one of the day.

clue.text: Salt, reefer, nautical, carrying plant

indicators.note: the run of words carries the answer inside it

parts.note: salT REEFER Nautical

explanation.surface: A list of seafaring words, a salt being an old sailor, alongside a cargo plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The seafaring words are camouflage: the answer runs across them, ignoring the commas.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree fern is a large fern with a trunk like a tree.
